parent: II. Explaining the Name of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 第二、翻釋不共名。不共名者，即是波羅蜜，亦為二意：一者、翻名；二者、解釋。就第一、翻名中略出三翻不同：一者、諸經論中多翻為到彼岸；二、《摩訶衍論》中別翻云事究竟；三、《瑞應經》中翻云度無極。
en: Second, translating the unshared name. The unshared name is "pāramitā" itself, and this too has two parts: translating the name; and explaining it. As to translating the name, here in brief are three differing renderings: first, most sūtras and treatises render it as "gone to the other shore"; second, the Mahāyāna treatise gives the distinct rendering "the completion of the task"; third, the Sūtra of Auspicious Manifestations renders it as "crossing to the limitless."

zh: 第二、釋此三翻，亦為二意：一、別；二、通。此皆對事理名義。第一、別釋，言到彼岸者，生死為此岸，涅槃為彼岸，煩惱為中流。菩薩以無相妙慧，乘禪定舟航，從生死此岸，度涅槃彼岸。故知約理定以明波羅蜜。言事究竟者，即是菩薩大悲，為眾生遍修一切事行滿足，故《摩訶衍》云：「菩薩因禪能究竟眾事，禪在菩薩心中，名波羅蜜。」此據事行說波羅蜜。言度無極者，通論事理，悉有幽遠之義，合而言之，故云度無極。此約事理行滿說波羅蜜。
en: Second, explaining these three renderings: this too has two parts — taken separately, and taken together. All of them correspond to the name and meaning of either phenomenal conduct or principle. First, taken separately: "gone to the other shore" — birth-and-death is this shore, nirvāṇa is the other shore, and affliction is the current running between them. The bodhisattva, by means of signless and wondrous wisdom, rides the vessel of dhyāna-concentration, crossing from this shore of birth-and-death to the other shore of nirvāṇa. Hence it can be known that this explains pāramitā in terms of principle and concentration. "The completion of the task" — this is the bodhisattva's great compassion, cultivating every practical conduct on behalf of sentient beings to its full completion. Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Through dhyāna, the bodhisattva is able to bring every task to completion; when dhyāna is held within the bodhisattva's mind, it is called pāramitā." This explains pāramitā in terms of phenomenal conduct. "Crossing to the limitless" — taken to cover both phenomenal conduct and principle together, both have the sense of the profound and far-reaching, and taken jointly, it is therefore called "crossing to the limitless." This explains pāramitā in terms of phenomenal conduct and principle both being fulfilled.

zh: 第二、通釋三翻，並得同對事理俱隨緣化物，故立異名。所以者何？若言無相之慧能度生死，故為理行者，今言理中，有佛無佛，性相常然，豈論無相之慧能度生死？終是就事作此說也。事究竟亦是從理立名者，若緣理而起事行，當知說事究竟亦是約理名波羅蜜度無極，亦未必一向就事理無極名波羅蜜。所以者何？諸佛隨緣利物，出沒不定，無極或時對事，或時對理，豈有定準？當知三名理事互通，未必偏有所屬，餘例可知。釋波羅蜜義，至下第十、結會歸趣中，自當廣明。
en: Second, explaining the three renderings taken together: all three can equally be said to correspond to both phenomenal conduct and principle, both following conditions to transform beings — hence different names are established for them. Why is this? If it is said that signless wisdom alone can cross birth-and-death, and this is therefore taken to be a matter of principle — yet within principle itself, whether a buddha appears or not, nature and characteristic remain ever the same; how, then, could one speak of signless wisdom crossing birth-and-death at all? In the end this too is a statement made in terms of phenomenal conduct. As for "the completion of the task" also being a name established from principle: if phenomenal conduct arises in dependence on principle, one should know that speaking of "the completion of the task" is also naming pāramitā in terms of principle. Nor does "crossing to the limitless" necessarily always name pāramitā in terms of phenomenal conduct and principle both being limitless. Why is this? The buddhas, following conditions to benefit beings, appear and withdraw without any fixed pattern; "the limitless" sometimes corresponds to phenomenal conduct, sometimes to principle — how could there be any fixed rule? One should know that these three names interpenetrate between principle and phenomenal conduct, and need not be assigned one-sidedly to only one or the other; the remaining cases may be understood by the same logic. The meaning of pāramitā will be explained fully further below, in the tenth topic, where the treatise is gathered together and its destination pointed out.

Zhiyi's three renderings of "pāramitā" line up with a recurring pair in this treatise — principle (理) and phenomenal conduct (事) — the same pair invoked back in topic 1's account of emptiness and the vow. "Gone to the other shore" leans toward principle (the destination itself, nirvāṇa); "the completion of the task" leans toward conduct (the bodhisattva's actual work for beings); "crossing to the limitless" is offered as covering both. True to form, Zhiyi then refuses to let the three stay neatly sorted, arguing that even "gone to the other shore" is, on inspection, a statement about conduct rather than a bare metaphysical claim about principle — principle itself, he says, "remains ever the same" whether or not a buddha appears to cross it.

items.en: Why Dhyāna Alone Is Called Pāramitā
parent: II. Explaining the Name of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 第三、料簡，如《摩訶衍論》中云：「問曰：背捨、勝處、一切處等，何故不名波羅蜜，獨稱禪為波羅蜜？答曰：禪最大如王，言禪波羅蜜者，一切皆攝。是四禪中，有八背捨、八勝處、十一切處、四無量心、五神通、練禪、自在定、十四變化心、無諍三昧、願智、頂禪、首楞嚴等諸三昧，百則有八，諸佛、不動等，百則二十，皆在禪中。若諸佛成道，轉法輪，入涅槃，所有勝妙功德悉在禪中，說禪則攝一切，若說餘定，則有所不攝，故禪名波羅蜜。復次，四禪中，智定等故，說波羅蜜。未到地、中間禪，智多而定少；四無色，定多而智少。如車輪，一強一弱，則不任載。四禪智定等故，說波羅蜜。復次，約禪說波羅蜜，則攝一切諸定。所以者何？禪，秦言思惟修。此諸定悉是思惟修功德故。」
en: Third, resolving points of doubt. As the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Question: Why are the liberations, the stations of mastery, the totality-bases, and the like not called pāramitā, while dhyāna alone is called pāramitā? Answer: Dhyāna is greatest of all, like a king; when we speak of 'dhyāna-pāramitā,' everything is thereby included. Within the four dhyānas are contained the eight liberations, the eight stations of mastery, the ten totality-bases, the four immeasurable minds, the five supernormal powers, the refining of dhyāna, the sovereign concentrations, the fourteen transformation-minds, the concentration free of contention, wish-wisdom, the summit-dhyānas, the Śūraṅgama and other samādhis — a hundred and eight of these — together with the buddhas' own samādhis, the unshakeable, and the rest — a hundred and twenty of these — all are contained within dhyāna. Since whatever sublime and wondrous merit belongs to the buddhas' accomplishing the path, turning the wheel of the Dharma, and entering nirvāṇa is, without exception, contained within dhyāna, to speak of dhyāna is to include everything; but to speak of any other concentration leaves something not included. Hence dhyāna alone receives the name pāramitā.

Furthermore: within the four dhyānas, wisdom and concentration are equal, and so it is called pāramitā. In the 'not-yet-arrived' state and in the intermediate dhyāna, wisdom is greater and concentration lesser; in the four formless absorptions, concentration is greater and wisdom lesser — like a cart whose two wheels are one strong and one weak, unable to bear its load. Since the four dhyānas have wisdom and concentration equal, they are called pāramitā.

Furthermore: to speak of pāramitā in terms of dhyāna is to include every concentration whatsoever. Why is this? 'Dhyāna,' in the language of the Qin dynasty, means 'contemplative cultivation' — and every one of these concentrations is, without exception, accomplished through the merit of contemplative cultivation."

zh: 當知諸定悉得受波羅蜜名。如《大品》中說百波羅蜜，亦說背捨、勝處等皆名波羅蜜，但四禪在根本，先受其名，非不通於餘定。問曰：上明禪、定、三昧、波羅蜜等，為同為異？答曰：通而為論，名義互通；別而往解，四法名義各有主對。所以者何？根本四禪但名禪，非定、三昧，亦不名波羅蜜。無色但名定，非禪、三昧，亦不名波羅蜜。未到地禪、中間，雖非正禪定，是方便故，或名禪，或名定，非三昧，亦不名波羅蜜。空、無相等，但名三昧，非禪、定，亦不名波羅蜜。背捨、勝處、六通、四辯等，具有禪、定、三昧等三法，而不名禪定、三昧，亦非波羅蜜。九次第定具有三法，但名為定，不名禪、三昧，亦非波羅蜜。有覺有觀，及師子、超越、無諍等，亦具三法，但名三昧，不名禪、定，亦非波羅蜜。願智頂等，具有三法，但名禪，不名定、三昧，亦非波羅蜜。九種大禪及首楞嚴等，並具四法，亦名禪，亦名定，亦名三昧，即是波羅蜜。若用首楞嚴心入前三法中，一切皆名波羅蜜，故百波羅蜜中一切法門皆名波羅蜜。
en: One should know from this that every concentration can, in fact, receive the name pāramitā. As the Larger Sūtra speaks of a hundred pāramitās, and also says that the liberations, the stations of mastery, and the rest are all called pāramitā — it is only that the four root dhyānas, being the foundation, receive the name first, not that the name fails to extend to the other concentrations as well.

Question: In the foregoing, "dhyāna," "concentration," "samādhi," and "pāramitā" have all been explained — are they the same, or different? Answer: Taken as a whole, their names and meanings interconnect; taken individually, each of these four terms has its own proper referent. Why is this? The root four dhyānas are called only "dhyāna" — not "concentration" or "samādhi," nor are they called "pāramitā." The formless absorptions are called only "concentration" — not "dhyāna" or "samādhi," nor are they called "pāramitā." The "not-yet-arrived" dhyāna and the intermediate dhyāna, though not concentration proper, being expedient means, may be called either "dhyāna" or "concentration," but not "samādhi," nor are they called "pāramitā." Emptiness, signlessness, and the like are called only "samādhi" — not "dhyāna" or "concentration," nor are they called "pāramitā." The liberations, the stations of mastery, the six supernormal powers, the four unhindered eloquences, and the like possess all three qualities of dhyāna, concentration, and samādhi, and yet are not called "dhyāna," "concentration," or "samādhi," nor are they "pāramitā." The nine sequential concentrations possess all three qualities, but are called only "concentration" — not "dhyāna" or "samādhi," nor are they "pāramitā." The samādhi possessing initial thought and sustained reflection, together with the lion's-sport concentration, the transcendence concentration, the concentration free of contention, and the like, likewise possess all three qualities, but are called only "samādhi" — not "dhyāna" or "concentration," nor are they "pāramitā." Wish-wisdom, the summit-dhyānas, and the like possess all three qualities, but are called only "dhyāna" — not "concentration" or "samādhi," nor are they "pāramitā." The nine kinds of great dhyāna, the Śūraṅgama, and the like alone possess all four qualities together — they are called "dhyāna," called "concentration," and called "samādhi" all at once: this is precisely "pāramitā." And if the mind of Śūraṅgama is brought to bear within the three preceding categories, every one of them can then also be called "pāramitā" — this is why, among the hundred pāramitās, every dharma-gate whatsoever can be called pāramitā.

zh: 今略對四法分別如前。若諸大聖善巧隨緣利物，則言無定準解釋（云云）。故諸經論中出沒立名，其意難見，不可謬執。而經論中多約禪明波羅蜜者，以根本四禪是眾行之本，一切內行功德皆因四禪發，依四禪而住，是以獨禪得受波羅蜜名。
en: Here, in brief, the four terms have been distinguished as above. Since the great sages skillfully follow conditions to benefit beings, there is no fixed standard governing how they are explained (and so on) — hence the various sūtras and treatises name things as they appear and recede, and their intent is not easily seen; one should not cling wrongly to any single reading. Yet the reason the sūtras and treatises most often explain pāramitā specifically in terms of dhyāna is that the root four dhyānas are the foundation of every practice: every inward practice and its merit is brought forth through the four dhyānas and abides in dependence on them — this is why dhyāna alone receives the name pāramitā.

This is a technical but important piece of classification: Zhiyi (quoting the Mahāyāna treatise) sorts every meditative state named in the canon into which of four overlapping terms — dhyāna, concentration, samādhi, pāramitā — actually apply to it, and shows that only the rarest states (the nine kinds of great dhyāna, the Śūraṅgama samādhi) qualify for all four at once. The practical point beneath the taxonomy: "pāramitā" is not a synonym for "meditative attainment" in general — it marks out states complete enough, in both wisdom and concentration together, to carry the name. The Śūraṅgama samādhi named here is the same samādhi at the center of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, translated elsewhere on this site — Zhiyi treats it as the paradigm case of a "complete" concentration.

items.en: Other Names for Dhyāna-Pāramitā, and a Bodhisattva's Claim to It
parent: II. Explaining the Name of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh:
問曰：禪波羅蜜但有一名，更有餘稱？答曰：如《涅槃》中說：「言佛性者，有五種名，亦名首楞嚴，亦名般若，亦名中道，亦名金剛三昧大涅槃，亦云禪波羅蜜，即是佛性。」故知諸餘經中所說種種勝妙法門，名字無量，皆是禪波羅蜜之異名，故《摩訶衍》偈說：
般若是一法，佛說種種名，
隨諸眾生類，為之立異字。
若人得般若，戲論心皆滅，
譬如日出時，朝露一時失。
以此類之，禪名豈不遍通？若其禪定不具足攝一切諸法，則非究竟，何得名波羅蜜義？
en:
Question: Does dhyāna-pāramitā have only this one name, or does it also go by other names? Answer: As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "As for what is called buddha-nature, it has five names: it is also called Śūraṅgama, also called prajñā, also called the middle way, also called the vajra-samādhi of great nirvāṇa, and also called dhyāna-pāramitā — and this is precisely buddha-nature." From this it can be known that the various sublime and wondrous dharma-gates spoken of, under measureless different names, throughout the rest of the sūtras are all alternate names for dhyāna-pāramitā. Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says in verse:
"Prajñā is a single Dharma; the Buddha speaks of it under many names,
Following the type of each sentient being, distinct terms are established for it.
If a person attains prajñā, every idly theorizing mind is extinguished at once,
Just as, when the sun rises, the morning dew vanishes all together."
Reasoning by this same kind of logic, how could the name "dhyāna" not extend everywhere? If dhyāna-concentration did not, in its completeness, include every dharma whatsoever, it would not be ultimate — how, then, could it be entitled to the meaning of "pāramitā"?

zh: 問曰：諸法實相、首楞嚴及到彼岸等，唯佛一人方稱究竟，菩薩所行禪定，云何名波羅蜜？答曰：因中說果故，隨分說故，頓教所明發心畢竟二不別故，以如是等眾多義故，菩薩所行禪定亦得名波羅蜜。
en: Question: The true reality of all dharmas, the Śūraṅgama, "gone to the other shore," and the like are said to be ultimate only in the Buddha alone — how, then, can the dhyāna-concentration practiced by a bodhisattva be called pāramitā? Answer: Because the fruit is spoken of within the cause; because it is spoken of according to one's own portion of the path; because, as the sudden teaching makes clear, the arising of the mind at the very start and its ultimate completion are, in the end, not two different things — for these and many similar reasons, the dhyāna-concentration practiced by a bodhisattva can indeed also be called pāramitā.

The closing move is a small but important piece of Tiantai doctrine in miniature: an apparent problem (only a buddha's realization is truly "ultimate," so how can a bodhisattva's still-imperfect dhyāna be called pāramitā, a word that means "gone all the way across"?) is resolved by appeal to what later Tiantai writing calls "the identity of beginning and end" — the sudden teaching's claim that the very first arising of the bodhi-mind and its final completion are, in principle, not two different things. This same move — the fruit already present, in some sense, within the cause — will recur through the rest of this treatise. This closes topic 2.

quiz.q: Among the three renderings of "pāramitā," where does "crossing to the limitless" come from?
options: the Abhidharma texts
the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra
the Mahāyāna treatise
the Sūtra of Auspicious Manifestations
quiz.why: "First, most sūtras and treatises render it as 'gone to the other shore'; second, the Mahāyāna treatise gives the distinct rendering 'the completion of the task'; third, the Sūtra of Auspicious Manifestations renders it as 'crossing to the limitless.'" The Abhidharma rendering, "the grove of merit and virtue," was for "dhyāna."

quiz.q: In explaining "gone to the other shore," what does the text say this shore, the other shore, and the current are?
options: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm
birth-and-death is this shore, nirvāṇa the other shore, affliction the current between
the scattered mind, the concentrated mind, and discursive thought
ordinary people, buddhas, and bodhisattvas
quiz.why: "Birth-and-death is this shore, nirvāṇa is the other shore, and affliction is the current running between them. The bodhisattva, by means of signless and wondrous wisdom, rides the vessel of dhyāna-concentration." Hence this rendering explains pāramitā in terms of principle and concentration.

quiz.q: Taken separately, "the completion of the task" explains pāramitā in terms of what?
options: phenomenal conduct: the bodhisattva's great compassion cultivating every practical conduct for beings to completion
principle and concentration: riding the vessel of dhyāna with signless wisdom
fruits: rebirth in heaven
both conduct and principle fulfilled
quiz.why: "'The completion of the task' — this is the bodhisattva's great compassion, cultivating every practical conduct on behalf of sentient beings to its full completion ... This explains pāramitā in terms of phenomenal conduct." "Gone to the other shore" concerns principle and concentration, and "crossing to the limitless" covers both.

quiz.q: Where does the text say the meaning of pāramitā will be explained fully?
options: the tenth topic, where the treatise is gathered together and its destination pointed out
the seventh topic, cultivation and realization
the fifth topic, dharma and mind
the third topic, the gates
quiz.why: "The meaning of pāramitā will be explained fully further below, in the tenth topic, where the treatise is gathered together and its destination pointed out."

quiz.q: Quoting the Mahāyāna treatise, why are the liberations, stations of mastery, and totality-bases not called pāramitā while dhyāna is?
options: the liberations have no merit
the liberations and the rest are non-Buddhist practices
the liberations are higher than dhyāna
dhyāna is greatest, like a king; speaking of dhyāna includes everything, while speaking of other concentrations leaves something out
quiz.why: "Dhyāna is greatest of all, like a king ... to speak of dhyāna is to include everything; but to speak of any other concentration leaves something not included. Hence dhyāna alone receives the name pāramitā." The liberations and the rest are contained within the four dhyānas; they are neither non-Buddhist nor higher than dhyāna.

quiz.q: The four dhyānas have wisdom and concentration equal. How are the not-yet-arrived state, the intermediate dhyāna, and the four formless absorptions described?
options: the reverse
the not-yet-arrived and intermediate: more wisdom, less concentration; the formless: more concentration, less wisdom — like a cart-wheel strong on one side, unable to bear its load
all three have wisdom and concentration equal
none of them has any wisdom
quiz.why: "In the 'not-yet-arrived' state and in the intermediate dhyāna, wisdom is greater and concentration lesser; in the four formless absorptions, concentration is greater and wisdom lesser — like a cart-wheel, one part strong and the other weak, unable to bear its load." The two are easily reversed; the formless absorptions are deep in concentration but weak in wisdom.

quiz.q: Among the concentrations said to be contained within the four dhyānas, which set of numbers is correct?
options: eight liberations, ten stations, eight totality-bases, fourteen transformation-minds
nine liberations, eight stations, ten totality-bases, twelve transformation-minds
eight liberations, eight stations, twelve totality-bases, ten transformation-minds
eight liberations, eight stations of mastery, ten totality-bases, fourteen transformation-minds
quiz.why: "Within the four dhyānas are contained the eight liberations, the eight stations of mastery, the ten totality-bases, the four immeasurable minds, the five supernormal powers, the refining of dhyāna, the sovereign concentrations, the fourteen transformation-minds."

quiz.q: If every concentration can receive the name pāramitā, why do the four dhyānas receive it first?
options: because the Buddha taught only the four dhyānas
because the four dhyānas are easiest
the four dhyānas are the root and foundation of every practice; every inward practice and merit arises through them and abides in them
because the other concentrations are practiced by non-Buddhists
quiz.why: "It is only that the four root dhyānas, being the foundation, receive the name first, not that the name fails to extend to the other concentrations as well." Later: "the root four dhyānas are the foundation of every practice: every inward practice and its merit is brought forth through the four dhyānas and abides in dependence on them." Ease and non-Buddhist practice have nothing to do with it.

quiz.q: Taken individually, what are the root four dhyānas called?
options: all four names together
only "concentration"
only "dhyāna" — not concentration or samādhi, nor pāramitā
only "samādhi"
quiz.why: "The root four dhyānas are called only 'dhyāna' — not 'concentration' or 'samādhi,' nor are they called 'pāramitā.'" All four names belong to the nine great dhyānas and the Śūraṅgama; "concentration" alone to the formless absorptions and nine sequential concentrations; "samādhi" alone to emptiness and signlessness.

quiz.q: Among the four terms, what are the formless absorptions called?
options: only "dhyāna"
only "samādhi"
either "dhyāna" or "concentration"
only "concentration"
quiz.why: "The formless absorptions are called only 'concentration' — not 'dhyāna' or 'samādhi,' nor are they called 'pāramitā.'" "Either dhyāna or concentration" describes the not-yet-arrived and intermediate dhyānas, as expedient means.

quiz.q: Among the four terms, what are emptiness, signlessness, and the like called?
options: precisely "pāramitā"
only "dhyāna"
only "samādhi"
only "concentration"
quiz.why: "Emptiness, signlessness, and the like are called only 'samādhi' — not 'dhyāna' or 'concentration,' nor are they called 'pāramitā.'"

quiz.q: The nine sequential concentrations and wish-wisdom with the summit-dhyānas each possess all three qualities. What is each called?
options: the nine sequential concentrations only "concentration"; wish-wisdom and summit-dhyānas only "dhyāna"
the reverse
both "pāramitā"
both only "samādhi"
quiz.why: "The nine sequential concentrations possess all three qualities, but are called only 'concentration' ... Wish-wisdom, the summit-dhyānas, and the like possess all three qualities, but are called only 'dhyāna.'" Those with all three but called only "samādhi" are dhyāna with discursive thought, the lion's-sport, transcendence, and contention-free concentrations.

quiz.q: Which states "possess all four qualities together," called dhyāna, concentration, and samādhi at once, and thus pāramitā?
options: the nine kinds of great dhyāna, the Śūraṅgama, and the like
the root four dhyānas
the nine sequential concentrations
the liberations, stations of mastery, six powers, four eloquences
quiz.why: "The nine kinds of great dhyāna, the Śūraṅgama, and the like alone possess all four qualities together ... this is precisely 'pāramitā.'" The liberations, stations of mastery, six powers, and four eloquences possess three qualities yet bear none of the names.

quiz.q: In the verse "Prajñā is a single Dharma; the Buddha speaks of it under many names," what image shows idle theorizing vanishing when prajñā is attained?
options: a great flame that cannot be grasped from any side
the morning dew vanishing all together when the sun rises
a lamp in the wind
a great rain settling the dust
quiz.why: The verse: "If a person attains prajñā, every idly theorizing mind is extinguished at once, / Just as, when the sun rises, the morning dew vanishes all together." The rain and dust belong to the earlier verse about dhyāna stilling discursive thought, the lamp in the wind to wisdom without concentration, and the great flame to a verse quoted in the fifth topic.

quiz.q: What does the text say would follow if dhyāna-concentration did not include every dharma in its completeness?
options: it could still be called pāramitā
it could only be called samādhi
one would have to switch to cultivating prajñā instead
it would not be ultimate, and could not be entitled to the name pāramitā
quiz.why: "If dhyāna-concentration did not, in its completeness, include every dharma whatsoever, it would not be ultimate — how, then, could it be entitled to the meaning of 'pāramitā'?" It is precisely because dhyāna includes everything that it deserves the name.

quiz.q: Asked how a bodhisattva's dhyāna can be called pāramitā when only the Buddha is ultimate, what reasons does the text give?
options: a bodhisattva's dhyāna cannot actually be called pāramitā
because the fruit is spoken of within the cause; because it is spoken of according to one's portion; because in the sudden teaching the first resolve and final completion are not two
because the bodhisattva's dhyāna is deeper than the Buddha's
because the bodhisattva has already become a buddha
quiz.why: "Because the fruit is spoken of within the cause; because it is spoken of according to one's own portion of the path; because, as the sudden teaching makes clear, the arising of the mind at the very start and its ultimate completion are, in the end, not two different things." The bodhisattva is not yet a buddha nor deeper than one, and the conclusion is that the name does apply.
